title: Cryobank Operations (Awareness Level)
desc: Understand how biological sample banks are run: consent, labelling, cold storage, records, security and ethics. Awareness only.
outcomes: Explain what a cryobank stores, why consent matters and how a sample is traced.
Complete a sample record and label with a two-person check.
Examine the cold chain and identify risks with controls.
Judge a bank's security, privacy and ethics policies for gaps.
Draft a daily operations checklist and run a mock audit.
task: Create a daily operations checklist and a sample record template for a practice cryobank, and run a mock audit.
condition: A computer, practice forms and a mentor. No real samples, personal data or hazardous materials are used.
standard: Checklist covers temperature, alarms, labelling, access and records; mock audit finds at least 3 planted errors; peers rate Meets or better.
who: Lab trainees, hospital store staff, health administrators.
evidence: checklist, record template, mock audit report
modules: What a cryobank holds
Understand

A cryobank is a managed store where biological samples are kept at about minus 80 to minus 196 degrees Celsius so they stay stable until an agreed use. It is a records business as much as a freezer business: a sample is only valuable if it can be found, identified and released to the right person.
Common holdings are blood cells, tissue pieces, cord blood, reproductive cells and research samples, each with storage rules and legal limits that differ by place.
Liquid nitrogen tanks hold near minus 196 degrees Celsius and mechanical freezers near minus 80, and the bank chooses by sample type and time kept.
Each sample has a custodian, a stated purpose, a storage period and written conditions for release or disposal.
Traceability means any sample can be located in under 10 minutes and its identity proved from the record.

A family stores cord blood for 20 years. The contract lists the storage period (20 years), who may ask for release (the guardian, then the child at 18), the renewal steps and where samples go if the bank closes. The record shows tank 2, rack B, box 4, slot 7.
Write a one-paragraph summary of what a cryobank stores, why consent matters and how one sample is found again, using the five contract items above.
Summary names consent, storage conditions and traceability, and uses at least four of the contract items.
Consent and ownership
Understand

Consent means a person understands what will happen to a sample and agrees freely. Without valid consent a bank cannot properly store, use or release a sample, so consent is checked before anything enters the freezer.
A plain-language form covers purpose, storage length, research use, risks, costs, disposal and the right to withdraw, written so the person can follow it.
A child's sample needs guardian consent and a dated plan to ask the person again at adulthood, often at 18, depending on local rules.
Each choice is a separate tick box and research use defaults to No, so silence never counts as agreement.
The signed form is scanned, given the sample ID and linked to the record; a withdrawal is logged with its date and acted on within the stated time.

A donor receives a form with 6 boxes. Research use defaults to No; she ticks Yes, anonymised only, signs and dates it. The reviewer matches form ID C-2031 to the label, finds all 6 boxes complete and files a scan the same day. Questions about local law go to a qualified legal adviser.
Review a practice consent form and list four gaps, each with a suggested fix and the reason it matters.
Four real gaps are found, each with a fix; no gap is invented and no legal advice is given.
Labelling and records
Apply
A sample without a correct label is a lost sample. Labels and records are the bank's memory, so every entry follows one fixed pattern and a second person checks it.
Every record holds a unique ID, date, sample type, volume, consent reference and full location in the order tank, rack, box, slot.
Two people check entry and removal: one reads the label aloud, the other reads the record, and both initial and time-stamp it.
Use a barcode plus a handwritten backup, because frost and wear can make a barcode unreadable.
Never reuse, overwrite or delete an ID; a mistake is crossed with one line, initialled and explained.

Operator A logs sample C-2031 as 2.0 ml cord blood, consent ref F-118, tank 2, rack B, box 4, slot 7. Checker B scans the barcode, reads the handwritten backup and both agree. Both sets of initials and the time 09:40 go on the record before the sample moves.
Fill five practice records with the full pattern, then swap with a peer who checks each one against its label.
Zero errors across five records, and every record carries two sets of initials and a time.
Cold chain and alarms
Analyse
The cold chain is the unbroken run of safe temperatures from collection to release. One failure can damage a whole tank within hours, so risks are found early and each gets a control and an owner.
Read and log temperature and nitrogen level at a set time each day, and compare today's figure with the last 7 days to spot drift.
Alarms need a call-out list of at least 3 names, a rule that someone answers within 15 minutes, and backup power for sensors.
Transport uses validated containers with a temperature logger, and the printout is attached to the record on arrival.
Test every alarm monthly and note the date, the result and who tested it.

A tank level falls from 60 percent to 52 percent in 7 days, faster than the usual 2 points a week. The log shows the trend, the owner orders a lid check and a refill, and the level returns to 60 percent. A night alarm at 02:10 reaches the second name when the first does not answer.
Mark five cold-chain risks on a practice floor plan and write one control and one named owner for each.
Every risk has a control, an owner and a test date; none is left as 'be careful'.
Safety for staff
Apply
Extreme cold and nitrogen are real hazards: cold burns, and oxygen loss in closed rooms. This module gives awareness only; real handling needs formal training from a qualified safety professional.
Wear insulated cryogenic gloves, a face shield and an apron when opening a tank, and keep sleeves and trousers covering skin.
An oxygen sensor in each nitrogen room sounds an alarm when oxygen falls below its set level, commonly near 19.5 percent, and the room is ventilated.
Never work alone in the store; use a buddy rule and a sign-in sheet, and learn two evacuation routes.
For a cold burn, staff follow the site first-aid plan and call the trained first aider or emergency services rather than improvise treatment.

The oxygen alarm sounds at 10:15. Both staff leave at once and close the door behind them, and the supervisor switches on ventilation from outside. They return only when a trained person confirms the portable monitor shows a safe reading. Time out of the room is 12 minutes and is logged.
Write five specific safety rules and one emergency drill that names who does what in the first 5 minutes.
Rules are specific and measurable, and the drill gives a named person for every step; no medical treatment is advised.
Security and privacy
Evaluate
Samples and the data linked to them are sensitive, so access is limited, logged and reviewed. A policy is judged by whether it can be checked, not by how strong its wording sounds.
Badge access is given by role; the list of badge holders is reviewed every 3 months and leavers are removed within 1 day.
Cameras cover doors and storage rooms but never private areas; visitors sign a log and are escorted at all times.
Identity data is kept apart from sample codes, only authorised staff can join the two, and every view is logged.
A breach, such as a lost badge or a wrongly shared record, is reported the same day to a named person and written up.

A reviewer scores a practice policy. Strengths (3): badge by role, escorted visitors, logged record views. Gaps (3): no leaver deadline, no breach contact, no log review. She suggests removal in 1 day, a named contact and a monthly log check.
Review a practice security policy and list three strengths and three gaps, each with a suggested fix.
Each strength and gap quotes the policy line it refers to, and fixes are specific and testable.
Ethics, fairness and cost
Evaluate
A bank asks people to trust it for years, often at a hopeful or worrying time. Ethics means honest claims, clear costs and fair treatment, so a person can decide without pressure.
Fees, renewal terms and extra charges are shown in writing before signing, with a cooling-off time to think.
No promise of future cures is made; claims about benefit use careful words and point people to qualified health professionals.
An exit plan explains where samples go if the bank closes, who pays, and how owners are told, at least 90 days ahead.
Staff respect different cultural, faith and family views about tissue and explain choices in plain language, in the person's language where possible.

A leaflet says 'may help treat many diseases'. The reviewer flags it as a misleading claim and rewrites it: 'Stored samples have limited, specific uses. Ask your doctor what applies to you.' The leaflet also has no exit plan, so the reviewer adds a question about it.
Write five ethics questions you would ask a bank, each tied to fees, claims, exit plans, consent or fair treatment.
Five questions are fair and specific and cover at least four of the five themes.
Checklist and mock audit
Create
Routine keeps samples safe, and an audit proves the routine works. You will build a checklist and then test it by finding errors planted by a peer.
Split tasks by rhythm: daily (temperature, level, alarm lights, door log), weekly (alarm test, label spot-check of 10 samples), monthly (record review, backup power test).
Each line has a tick, initials, a time and a space for a problem; a blank line means not done.
An audit trail follows 3 samples from consent to location and checks every signature on the way.
Each fault gets a corrective action with an owner and a due date, and the checklist is reviewed monthly.

A peer plants 3 errors: a missing second-person check, a temperature entry made 4 hours late, and an unlabelled box. The auditor finds all 3 in 25 minutes and writes actions: retrain on the two-person check by Friday, set a 09:00 reminder, relabel and verify with a second person today.
Draft the checklist, plant three errors in a practice record set for a peer, then run the audit and write the report.
Checklist covers temperature, alarms, labelling, access and records; all three planted errors are found, each with an action, owner and date.
quiz: What does a cryobank store?

It stores biological samples such as cells, tissue, cord blood, reproductive cells and research samples at very low temperatures, with records showing who owns each sample, why it is kept and how it can be found again. (Covered in module 1: What a cryobank holds. To pass that module: Summary names consent, storage conditions and traceability, and uses at least four of the contract items.)
Why are two-person checks used?

A second person reads the label against the record, which catches a wrong ID or slot before a sample moves, and two sets of initials show who was responsible. (Covered in module 3: Labelling and records. To pass that module: Zero errors across five records, and every record carries two sets of initials and a time.)
Name one cold-chain risk and a control for it.

A power cut or low nitrogen can warm samples; controls include a daily level log, alarms with a call-out list and backup power. (Covered in module 4: Cold chain and alarms. To pass that module: Every risk has a control, an owner and a test date; none is left as 'be careful'.)
Name one staff safety rule and say why it matters.

Never work alone in a nitrogen store and leave at once if the oxygen alarm sounds, because nitrogen can push out air in a closed room. (Covered in module 5: Safety for staff. To pass that module: Rules are specific and measurable, and the drill gives a named person for every step; no medical treatment is advised.)
Who may access identity data?

Only authorised staff whose role needs it, with every view logged, and with identity kept apart from sample codes. (Covered in module 6: Security and privacy. To pass that module: Each strength and gap quotes the policy line it refers to, and fixes are specific and testable.)
What does valid consent include?

Purpose, how long the sample is kept, any research use, risks, costs, disposal and the right to withdraw, in plain language and signed and dated. (Covered in module 2: Consent and ownership. To pass that module: Four real gaps are found, each with a fix; no gap is invented and no legal advice is given.)
Why keep backup labels?

Frost, cold and wear can make a barcode unreadable, so a handwritten label and paper record still let staff prove identity. (Covered in module 3: Labelling and records. To pass that module: Zero errors across five records, and every record carries two sets of initials and a time.)
What is an exit plan?

A written plan for moving samples to another licensed bank if the bank closes, saying who pays and how owners are told. (Covered in module 7: Ethics, fairness and cost. To pass that module: Five questions are fair and specific and cover at least four of the five themes.)
What is an audit trail?

A dated record of who did what and when, so a reviewer can follow a sample from consent to storage and release. (Covered in module 8: Checklist and mock audit. To pass that module: Checklist covers temperature, alarms, labelling, access and records; all three planted errors are found, each with an action, owner and date.)
Why keep logs?

Logs show that checks happened, reveal trends such as falling nitrogen, and let auditors find faults and prove they were fixed. (Covered in module 8: Checklist and mock audit. To pass that module: Checklist covers temperature, alarms, labelling, access and records; all three planted errors are found, each with an action, owner and date.)
